A bronco is a wild or only partially tamed horse — one that has not been fully trained to accept a rider or human control. The word almost always refers to horses found in the open ranges and plains of the American West.
What makes a bronco different from a regular horse?

Most horses you see in stables or on farms have been broken — a word used in horsemanship that means trained, not harmed. A broken horse has learned to accept a saddle, a rider, and commands. It is calm and cooperative.

A bronco is the opposite. It is unbroken or only loosely tamed. It is not used to carrying a rider, and when someone tries to ride it, the horse reacts instinctively — by bucking. Bucking means the horse violently arches its back, leaps into the air, and kicks its hind legs upward, doing everything it can to throw the rider off. This is the defining behavior that makes a bronco a bronco.
Where does the word get used?

1. In ranching and cowboy culture
On the open ranges of the American West, wild horses sometimes roamed freely. Cowboys who worked on ranches would sometimes have to catch and tame these horses. Before they were tamed, these horses were called broncos. Breaking a bronco — training a wild horse until it became manageable — was a real and important skill.

2. In rodeos
A rodeo is a competitive event that grew out of the skills real cowboys needed. One of the most iconic rodeo events is bronc riding (a shortened form of bronco riding). A cowboy climbs onto a bucking bronco and tries to stay on for eight full seconds while the horse bucks as hard as it can. It is considered one of the most difficult and dangerous rodeo events. There are two versions:

  • Bareback bronc riding — the rider holds on with one hand using a simple rigging strap, with no saddle.
  • Saddle bronc riding — the rider uses a specialized saddle and holds a rein attached to the horse's head.

3. As a general term for a spirited or difficult horse
Even outside the rodeo, people sometimes use "bronco" loosely to describe any horse that is feisty, unruly, or hard to control — not necessarily a fully wild horse, but one with a rebellious, untamed spirit.
Key qualities associated with a bronco

• Wild and free-spirited — not domesticated in the way a farm horse is
  • Resistant to riders — bucks, rears, twists, and fights against being ridden
  • Strong and energetic — broncos are not weak or passive; they are powerful animals
  • Unpredictable — you cannot easily predict what a bronco will do next, which is part of what makes them dangerous
How it is used in a sentence

• "The cowboy struggled to stay on the bronco as it bucked wildly across the arena."
  • "They brought in a bronco from the wild and spent weeks trying to break it."
  • "He was thrown off the bronco before the eight-second buzzer sounded."

The word has moved beyond horses and entered broader culture. The Denver Broncos — a famous American football team — take their name from this word, chosen to represent toughness, wildness, and power. The Ford Bronco is a rugged off-road vehicle whose name was chosen for the same reasons — to suggest something strong, untamed, and built for rough terrain. Whenever a brand or team picks the name "bronco," they are borrowing exactly these qualities: wild, powerful, hard to stop.

A bronco is a wild, unbroken horse known for bucking violently when ridden. It lives at the center of American Western and cowboy culture, and it represents the untamed, raw power of nature before humans have shaped it into obedience. Whether you see it at a rodeo or hear the word used figuratively, it always carries that core meaning: something fierce, free, and resistant to being controlled.
